title: How a retrieved passage changes an answer
subtitle: The claim, the concept, the evidence, the recap
thesis: An answer is only trustworthy when the reader can open the source behind it; retrieval is what makes that possible.

evidence.label: Illustrative dataset for layout demonstration — not measured production data.
Method: held-out questions, single reviewer, one fixed prompt
Practitioner guidance: cite the passage, not just the conclusion

sections.heading: The claim
sections.summary: An answer your reader cannot check is a claim, not a result — and the difference is visible panel by panel.
paragraphs: An answer your reader cannot check is a claim, not a result. The panels that follow show what changes when the source travels with the answer.
bullets: The difference is what the reader can open

sections.heading: The concept
sections.summary: Keep the question as written, look up passages that match it, and let the answer use only those passages.
paragraphs: Instead of answering from memory, the system looks up passages that match the question and constrains the answer to them. The question is kept as written so it can be compared with what was actually asked.

sections.heading: Answers with a checkable source
sections.summary: Across 1,200 illustrative questions, 78 percent of answers came back with a passage the reader could open.

sections.heading: Two ways to answer
sections.summary: Retrieval changes where the words come from, what the reader can open, and how quickly a fix reaches the answer.

sections.heading: Checkable answers by passage count
sections.summary: The share of checkable answers rises through about eight passages and then flattens.

sections.heading: Read with care
sections.summary: These figures are illustrative, come from a single reviewer, and do not measure a production system.
paragraphs: The figures on these panels are illustrative and were not measured in production. A single reviewer scored the run, so differences of a few points are inside the scoring noise.

sections.heading: Recap
sections.summary: Keep the source attached to the answer: it costs latency, but it replaces confident recall with something a reader can open.
paragraphs: The whole argument fits in one line. If the reader cannot open the source, the statement is a claim; attaching the passage turns it into a result, and the evidence panels show what that costs.
bullets: Show the reader where it came from
